title: Why Older Homes Have Worse Indoor Air Quality
h1: Why Do Older Homes Often Have Worse Indoor Air Quality?
description: Why older homes often have worse indoor air: aging ducts, attic leaks, old insulation, weak ventilation and outdated equipment, plus the fixes that help most.
quick_answer: Older homes often have leaky or deteriorating ducts, old or contaminated attic insulation, weak exhaust ventilation and aging HVAC equipment with basic filtration. That combination pulls attic and crawl space dust into the air and lets moisture and odors linger. Sealing and cleaning ducts, upgrading filtration and improving ventilation make the biggest difference.
body:
What makes older homes harder on indoor air?

Older doesn't automatically mean worse, but certain problems build up over decades. In San Diego and Orange County, many older homes are stucco tract houses with the furnace or air handler and ducts in the attic, and those systems have had a long time to collect problems.

  • Aging ductwork. Old flex duct gets brittle, tears and sags. Tape fails at joints. Leaky returns pull in attic dust and insulation fibers.
  • Old attic insulation. It may be thin, matted, dusty, or contaminated by rodents over the years.
  • Weak ventilation. Bathroom fans may be missing, undersized or venting into the attic. Kitchen hoods may just recirculate.
  • Basic filtration. Older systems often have a thin filter in a loose slot, or a filter grille that lets air bypass.
  • Years of buildup. Dust, dander and smoke residue from past occupants sit in ducts and carpets.

Are older homes drafty or stuffy?

Often both. Older homes leak a lot of air, but the leaks are in the wrong places. Air comes in from the attic, garage and crawl space, which are dusty and sometimes fume-filled, instead of fresh outdoor air from a controlled source. At the same time, without good exhaust fans, moisture and cooking odors don't have an easy way out.

That's why an older home can feel drafty on a cold inland night and still smell stale.

What about materials in older homes?

Homes built several decades ago may contain materials that are no longer used, such as asbestos in some duct wrap, popcorn ceilings, flooring or old furnace components, and lead in older paint. These are usually stable when left alone, but they become a concern when they're damaged, sanded or disturbed during repairs.

If your home is older and you're planning duct replacement, attic work or a remodel, ask about testing suspicious materials first. A good contractor will stop and recommend testing rather than tearing into something unknown.

Does old HVAC equipment affect air quality?

It can. Older furnaces and AC systems often have:

  • Dirty blowers and coils that have never been fully cleaned
  • Rusty drain pans that hold water and grow mold
  • Single-speed blowers that cycle on and off, with less filtering time
  • Furnace venting that should be checked for cracks or poor draft

Any home with a gas furnace or water heater needs working carbon monoxide alarms. If an alarm sounds, get everyone outside and call 911. If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside.

Do crawl spaces affect air in older homes?

Many older homes in coastal neighborhoods sit over a crawl space instead of a slab. Crawl spaces can be damp, and air from them moves up into the house through gaps around pipes, wiring and floor registers. If ducts run through the crawl space and leak, that musty air gets pulled straight into the system. A vapor barrier on the soil, sealed ducts and sealed floor penetrations keep most of that musty air out of the living space.

What fixes help an older home most?

  1. Seal or replace failing ducts. This stops attic air from being pulled into the system. Ducts that are torn or crushed are often better replaced than patched.
  2. Clean the ducts and system to clear out decades of buildup.
  3. Upgrade filtration with a properly fitted filter, or a media filter cabinet if the system can handle it.
  4. Fix ventilation. Make sure bathroom and kitchen fans work and vent outdoors.
  5. Clean up the attic. Remove contaminated insulation, seal air leaks and add fresh insulation.
  6. Control humidity, especially in coastal homes with crawl spaces.

Where should you start?

Start with an inspection of the ducts and attic, since that's where most of the problems in older homes begin. From there you can decide whether cleaning, sealing or full duct replacement makes sense.

faqs: How old is too old for air ducts?

There isn't a fixed age, but flex duct in a hot attic often starts breaking down after a couple of decades. Signs it's time to replace include tears, brittle outer jackets, sagging runs, crushed sections and joints that have come apart. Metal ducts can last longer if they're sealed and insulated.
Should I test for asbestos before duct work in an older home?

If the home is older and you see old duct wrap, tape or insulation that might contain asbestos, have it tested before anyone disturbs it. Asbestos is mainly a hazard when it's damaged or disturbed, so testing first protects you and the crew.
Will a new HVAC system fix air quality in an older home?

Not by itself. New equipment helps, but if it's connected to old, leaky ducts, it will still pull in attic dust. The best results come from addressing the ducts, filtration and ventilation along with the equipment.
Why does my older home smell musty?

Common causes are moisture in a crawl space, mold on the AC coil or in the drain pan, leaky ducts drawing in damp air, or old carpet and insulation holding odors. If the smell is strongest when the system runs, start by checking the HVAC system and ducts.
